## 2

I understand why you might be skeptical, especially since we usually rely on other people and institutions for information. But the evidence for a spherical Earth doesn’t depend only on photographs from space. Ships disappear over the horizon from the bottom up, different stars are visible at different latitudes, Earth’s shadow on the Moon during lunar eclipses is round, and people have measured the planet’s shape and circumference for thousands of years. Modern satellite systems, GPS, global time zones, and independent observations by people around the world also fit a spherical Earth far better than a flat one. What evidence would you find convincing?

## 3

Sunlight may look white, but it is actually made of many colors mixed together—like the colors in a rainbow. When sunlight enters Earth’s atmosphere, it bumps into tiny air molecules. Blue light gets scattered in all directions more easily than most other colors, so blue light spreads across the sky and reaches our eyes from many directions.

At sunrise and sunset, sunlight travels through more atmosphere. Much of the blue light gets scattered away before it reaches us, leaving more red, orange, and pink light—which is why the sky can look so colorful then.
